title: Stack With Instant Minimum
statement:
Build a stack of integers that can also report its smallest value at any moment.

  • MinStack() creates an empty stack.
  • push(val) puts val on top.
  • pop() removes the top value.
  • top() returns the top value without removing it.
  • getMin() returns the smallest value currently in the stack.

Every operation must run in O(1) time, including getMin right after a pop removed the old minimum. pop, top and getMin are only called when the stack is not empty.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the stack. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Once 8 and then 2 are popped, the minimum goes back to 5. A single "smallest so far" variable would still say 2.
The minimum 3 is pushed twice. Popping one copy must not forget the other, so equal values need their own record.

constraints: pop, top and getMin are only called on a non-empty stack
hints: Keeping one "current minimum" variable works for push. What goes wrong on pop?
When the minimum is popped, you need the minimum of what is left — the value it was before that element was pushed. Can you remember that at push time?
Store, next to every value, the minimum of the stack up to and including it. The top entry then always knows the current minimum.

explain.intuition:
A stack only ever changes at the top, so the stack below any element never changes while that element sits there. That means the minimum "from here down" is fixed the moment you push. Save it next to the value: (value, min so far).

Popping then rolls the minimum back automatically: the new top entry already holds the minimum of everything beneath it. It works like an undo history, where each entry remembers the state at the time it was made.
steps: Keep one stack of pairs [value, minSoFar].
push(val): the new minimum is val if the stack is empty, otherwise the smaller of val and the top's minSoFar. Push the pair.
pop(): pop the top pair. Nothing else to fix.
top() returns the top pair's value; getMin() returns the top pair's minSoFar.
pitfalls: Tracking the minimum in one variable: after the minimum is popped you have no way to know the next smallest without scanning.
With a separate stack of minimums, pushing only when val < currentMin. Duplicates of the minimum then share one entry, and popping one copy loses the other. Use <=.
Comparing against the top of an empty minimum stack on the very first push.

solutions.title: Plain stack, scan for the minimum
solutions.idea: Store values only and scan the whole stack in getMin. Correct, but getMin is O(n), which breaks the requirement.

solutions.title: Each entry remembers the minimum below it
solutions.idea: Push pairs (value, minimum so far). The top pair always holds the current minimum, and popping restores the previous one for free.

solutions.title: Second stack of minimums
solutions.idea: Keep the values on one stack and, on another, only the values that were a new minimum (or tied it) when pushed. Pop from the second stack when its top leaves the first.

followups: Also support getMax in O(1). Does the same trick extend?
Build a queue with O(1) amortized getMin. Hint: a queue can be made from two stacks.
